candidateRows: God's moral law reveals human guilt, while Jesus's death pays the guilty person's penalty and permits just forgiveness.
This supplies the pro side's central explanation of sin, judgment, substitutionary atonement, and the claimed justice of salvation.
Ray begins his opening by directing the gospel presentation toward Matt, moving from moral guilt under the commandments to the courtroom analogy of Christ paying a fine.
Death is the divinely imposed wage of sin and demonstrates that every sinner stands under a deserved sentence before judgment.
The claim explains why sin allegedly requires a grave penalty and therefore supports the necessity and moral proportionality of atonement.
After explaining that Jesus paid the sinner's fine, Ray interprets mortality as earned punishment for sin and as evidence of coming divine judgment.
The gospel becomes intelligible once a person humbly recognizes the seriousness of sin, repents, and trusts Christ for eternal life.
This directly answers the motion from the pro side by identifying moral self-knowledge as the condition under which atonement and salvation make sense.
Ray develops an extended speeding-fine analogy, contrasts pride with acknowledgment of guilt, and concludes by urging repentance and trust in the Savior.
Original sin cannot fairly be blamed on humanity if an omniscient God knowingly selected a creation in which human disobedience was inevitable.
This challenges the explanatory and moral foundation of the gospel by relocating responsibility for the fall from humanity to the creating deity.
Ray's account of human lawbreaking and the speeding-sign analogy used to establish guilt
Matt first questions whether any recognizable divine authority supplied the alleged moral rules, then argues that foreknowledge and creative choice make God responsible for original sin.
Inherited sin is morally incoherent because it assigns people guilt and punishment for conduct committed by others before they were born.
The argument attacks the justice of the inherited human predicament that the gospel presents as requiring universal rescue through atonement.
Matt distinguishes personal wrongdoing from inherited guilt and compares the latter to being beaten for an offense one did not actually commit.
Jesus's sacrifice is an unnecessary blood ritual because a rule-making and enforcing God could simply forgive without sacrificing himself to himself.
This directly contests whether substitutionary atonement makes moral or explanatory sense and proposes straightforward forgiveness as an available alternative.
Ray's claim that Jesus paid humanity's penalty so God could forgive guilty sinners justly
Matt connects animal sacrifice with blood magic, treats Jesus as a special instance of that system, and questions both its necessity and its evidential basis.
A wise and powerful God seeking fellowship could create suitable people with him directly, making the gospel's history of suffering, damnation, and rescue needlessly inefficient.
The argument tests the gospel as an explanatory plan against simpler divine alternatives and concludes that its complexity and hiddenness count against divine wisdom.
Matt asks what goal God is pursuing, contrasts the biblical sequence with direct creation in heaven, and argues that diminishing divine detectability worsens the proposed model.
If earthly life is intended to teach people, God's absence makes it inferior to instruction with an available teacher and therefore a poorly designed plan.
This addresses a plausible explanation for earthly struggle and argues that divine hiddenness makes the purported educational mechanism needlessly ineffective.
Matt considers whether hard experience is educational, contrasts it with guided teaching, and uses a grocery-store analogy to characterize an absent designer's method.
God has supplied evidence of moral authority through a divinely written conscience whose basic moral knowledge persists even when socially shaped or seared.
The response attempts to supply the missing epistemic link between divine law and human culpability on which Ray's account of sin and atonement depends.
Matt's objection that no recognized divine authority supplied signs or enforceable moral rules
Ray answers the missing-signs objection by appealing to conscience, acknowledges social shaping, and claims biblical searing explains divergent moral judgments.
A scriptural assertion about another person's inner knowledge cannot override that person's contrary report and provides no independent reason to accept the assertion.
This challenges the epistemic method used to establish universal awareness of God and guilt, weakening the claimed basis for culpability and needed salvation.
Ray's repeated claim that Matt knows God exists and knows alleged blasphemy is morally wrong
Matt rejects Ray's claims about his mental state; after Ray grounds them in the Bible, Matt points out that possessing such a book does not make its claims infallible.
An omniscient creator who selected this universe over alternatives bears ultimate responsibility for creating the conditions in which Matt remains a nonbeliever.
The argument directly challenges the coherence of divine judgment by placing responsibility for disbelief on an omniscient creator who selected the realized world.
Ray's claims that God created the world, knows every outcome, and nevertheless holds human beings responsible.
After securing agreement about omniscience and possible alternative worlds, Matt infers that God's selection of this world makes God ultimately responsible for his nonbelief.
Divine foreknowledge or original sin does not excuse a person's wrongdoing, just as blaming God would not defeat responsibility for a serious crime in court.
This is Ray's principal response to the responsibility objection and attempts to preserve individual culpability despite God's knowledge and creative choice.
Matt's argument that God's choice of which possible universe to create transfers ultimate responsibility for nonbelief to God.
Ray answers the possible-world argument with a legal analogy in which a guilty defendant cannot avoid personal responsibility by claiming that God caused the offense.
The objection concerns responsibility internal to Ray's model, not a real-world denial of personal agency; on that model God's exhaustive plan leaves no free will or individual responsibility.
The clarification exposes the courtroom analogy as addressing a different claim and renews the central challenge to the moral coherence of divine judgment.
Ray's courtroom analogy portraying Matt's objection as an attempt to excuse personal wrongdoing by blaming God.
Matt explains that he is evaluating the consequences of Ray's theology: if God selected and planned the world containing Matt's nonbelief, the model undermines free will and responsibility.
Atheism is only the absence of belief that a god exists, not a worldview or a scientific claim that nothing created everything.
The distinction prevents Ray from substituting cosmological claims associated with other atheists for Matt's actual position and defines the burden relevant to the debate.
Ray's proposed definition of an atheist as someone committed to the claim that nothing scientifically created everything.
Matt separates atheism from scientific, supernatural, and cosmological views, noting that atheists may hold many unrelated positions and that Ray already knows Matt's usage.
Matt's former Christianity was a false conversion because he did not truly repent, so his later departure does not disconfirm the gospel's promise of knowing God.
This move supplies Ray's explanation for apparent failed conversion and protects his experiential account of salvation from Matt's personal counterexample.
Matt's demand for a reliable way to determine whether Ray is right about the gospel and whether conversion genuinely reveals God.
Ray says the gospel must be obeyed and characterizes Matt as someone inoculated against truth by an insincere conversion that collapsed under later difficulty.
Although Matt now denies that anyone has a relationship with the risen Christ, his former Christian belief was sincere, and dismissing it as false does not establish Christianity's truth.
The distinction challenges the unfalsifiable use of true conversion and argues that reclassifying apostates cannot serve as evidence that the gospel is correct.
Ray's assertion that Matt's Christianity was merely a false conversion caused by failure to repent truly.
Matt concedes that he now rejects the reality of his former perceived relationship but maintains that his belief was sincere and publicly recognized by family and church acquaintances.
The existence of creation is self-evident proof of a creator, just as a building or painting is evidence of its maker.
This is Ray's primary positive evidential basis for God's existence, which underwrites the divine authority, judgment, and gospel claims disputed throughout the debate.
Matt's objection that quoting scripture does not make it true and that he is requesting evidence rather than refusing belief.
In response to Matt's request for evidence, Ray presents the natural world as creation whose existence necessarily points to a creator, paralleling familiar human artifacts.
Design cannot be inferred merely by labeling something a creation; investigators distinguish intentional structures from natural formations through comparative evidence and observable traces.
The argument directly attacks the inference from universe to creator by explaining that design recognition requires independent evidence rather than assumed creative origin.
Ray's assertion that buildings, paintings, and the universe transparently count as creations and therefore axiomatically require creators.
Matt contrasts designed and naturally occurring structures, explaining how physical marks, comparison, and further investigation can justify a design inference without presupposing one.
Declaring a past conversion inauthentic whenever a believer later leaves makes the conversion model immune to disconfirmation and substitutes unreliable common sense for evidence.
This objection identifies the self-sealing structure of Ray's salvation account and challenges its ability to explain failed conversions in an evidentially meaningful way.
Ray's claim that Matt's prior attempt at repentance failed because Matt obviously did not repent truly.
Matt argues that Ray preserves his model by redefining Matt's years of perceived salvation and spiritual experience as unreal solely because Matt later fell away.
The rich ruler passage does not teach salvation by moral works or selling possessions; commandments reveal sin, while eternal life comes by repentance, faith in Jesus, and divine grace.
The move directly articulates Ray's account of how salvation operates and answers a scriptural challenge to the explanatory coherence of the gospel message.
Matt's reading of Jesus' encounter with the rich ruler as teaching that keeping selected commandments and relinquishing possessions secures salvation.
Ray interprets the added prohibition on fraud as tailored to the ruler, then argues that neither restitution nor commandment keeping earns life because the law exposes sin and salvation is gracious.
Faith is an excuse for belief without good reasons, whereas confidence rests on evidence.
The distinction directly challenges the epistemic foundation offered for belief in God and the gospel.
Comfort's claim that accepting evidence about marriage also amounts to having faith.
Dillahunty distinguishes evidence-based confidence from faith while disputing the analogy between a demonstrable marriage and a relationship with God.
Scriptural inspiration attributed to God may instead be an undemonstrated product of the believer's own mind.
The argument challenges whether claimed divine communication can be distinguished from ordinary human cognition.
Comfort's assertion that God communicates with him daily through scripture.
After Comfort describes scripture as God's daily communication, Dillahunty asks how an outsider could distinguish conflicting claimed messages and determine which is genuine.
Using scripture to establish scripture's truth assumes the very conclusion that is being questioned.
It identifies circularity in the offered method for validating the religious authority underlying the gospel account.
Comfort's proposal that one should search scripture to decide which alleged divine message is correct.
Dillahunty argues that consulting scripture cannot resolve whether scripture is true when the proposed method begins by presuming its authority.
A person should begin with humble faith and ask God for instruction through scripture.
Comfort presents humility and initial faith as the practical route by which scripture and the gospel become intelligible.
Dillahunty's objection that scripture cannot be validated by first assuming scripture is true.
Comfort answers the circularity objection by prescribing a small beginning of faith, humble reading, and a request that God teach through the text.
Faith cannot demonstrate God, divine lawgiving, or scriptural truth and is therefore not a reliable pathway to truth.
The move attacks the explanatory and epistemic basis of the gospel by arguing that its foundational claims remain unsupported.
Comfort's instruction to repent and trust Christ before expecting scripture to make sense.
Dillahunty rejects Comfort's reliance on faith, says claims about his inner state are irrelevant, and argues that no sound method has been supplied for establishing God or scripture.
Human suffering, disease, and death corroborate the biblical teaching that creation is fallen.
The argument offers a central Christian explanation of suffering and treats observed evil as confirmation rather than disconfirmation of scripture.
The audience challenge that a tri-omni God permitting severe suffering would be responsible and unjust.
In response to childhood cancer and broader evil, Comfort generalizes to pervasive suffering and argues that these conditions substantiate the biblical account of a fallen world.
God is not responsible for human atrocities because perpetrators answer for their own sins at divine judgment.
The move defends divine justice and connects personal moral accountability directly to humanity's need for a savior.
The audience argument that knowingly creating a future wrongdoer makes God responsible for that person's actions.
Comfort denies that foreknowledge and creation transfer responsibility from human offenders to God, then invokes final judgment and the seriousness of sin to explain the need for salvation.
A creator who could have made a different universe bears responsibility for preventable atrocities within the universe chosen.
The argument directly challenges the coherence of absolving an omnipotent creator from responsibility for foreseeable and avoidable evil.
Comfort's denial that God is responsible for atrocities committed by people whom God knowingly created.
Dillahunty argues that Comfort's own acknowledgment of divine creative choice entails responsibility because God could have selected a world in which the atrocity never occurred.
Paying another person's debt removes the debt but does not repair the wrongdoer's defective character or stop repeated wrongdoing.
The analogy targets substitutionary atonement by separating compensation for harm from moral transformation of the person who caused it.
The debt-payment analogy asking how third-party payment changes the debtor's continuing untrustworthiness.

Dillahunty distinguishes discharge of an obligation from correction of character, using unpaid bills and repeated window-breaking to argue that substitution does not solve the underlying moral problem.
The claimed relationship with God lacks the demonstrable evidence available for ordinary factual claims such as having been married.
The argument returns to the debate's foundational evidential dispute and assigns the burden to the person seeking acceptance of the divine claim.
Comfort's comparison between certainty about God's revelation and Dillahunty's certainty that he had been married.

After clarifying ordinary knowledge rather than absolute certainty, Dillahunty argues that marriage can be demonstrated while God's existence cannot, and that persuasion requires meeting the burden of proof.
Christian conviction arises through a transforming encounter with God, after which Scripture becomes intelligible and internally harmonious.
The move supplies Ray's principal epistemic account of conversion and explains why he regards spiritual rebirth as prior to understanding the gospel texts.
The question challenges whether accepting the gospels without first investigating their evidential support is justified.
During audience questions, Ray distinguishes his conversion from belief produced by biblical investigation and grounds his confidence in personal transformation by God.
Christianity uniquely treats humans as guilty before a holy judge and offers salvation through divine mercy made legally possible by Christ's sacrificial death and resurrection.
This is a direct constructive account of sin, judgment, substitutionary sacrifice, mercy, and eternal salvation, covering the central components of the motion.
The audience question asks what makes Christianity more correct than other religions that also claim exclusive truth.
Ray contrasts Christianity with works-based religions, frames good works as attempted bribery of a just judge, and presents Christ's sacrifice as the basis for acquittal and eternal life.
Sinners deserve the loss imposed at judgment, and when reason cannot resolve the severity of that outcome, believers should trust that God will act rightly.
The response directly addresses the moral status of damnation, divine judgment, deserved punishment, and the reliance on God's righteousness central to the motion.
The audience question directly challenges whether sinners morally deserve punishment in the form of unending torment.
Ray answers a question about hell by describing earthly goods as divine gifts withdrawn at judgment and by appealing to trust in God's ultimate justice.
Atheism is not a worldview but a label for lacking belief in gods, while reliable understanding instead comes from science, logic, reason, and evidence.
The move rejects the burden placed on atheism to explain reality and states the alternative epistemic methods underlying Matt's skeptical critique of the gospel.
The audience question claims Matt stands behind atheism even though atheism cannot explain what exists.
Matt distinguishes an absence of god-belief from a comprehensive worldview and identifies science, logic, argument, and sound epistemology as his positive intellectual commitments.
Belief in the resurrection rests on experiential revelation by the living Christ, available to those who repent, trust Christ as sin-bearer, and obey him.
The resurrection is essential to Ray's account of atonement and salvation, and this move states his principal experiential warrant for accepting it as true.
The audience question challenges the resurrection by citing gospel controversy and the added ending of Mark.
Rather than defend gospel manuscripts historically, Ray says the risen Christ reveals himself personally and presents repentance and trust as the route to confirming the claim.
Ray's promised path to belief is insulated from failure because any sincere seeker who remains unconvinced can be blamed for doing it incorrectly.
The move attacks the falsifiability and evidential force of Ray's experiential salvation test, undermining a principal offered warrant for the gospel's truth.
Ray claims that anyone who repents, trusts Christ, and follows the promise will personally know the gospel is true.
Matt argues that the proposed test cannot count against Christianity because failed conversion is attributed to the seeker while God's promise is protected from disconfirmation.
A worldview should be accepted for correct, evidence-compatible explanations, not merely for explaining everything, and honestly leaving origins unresolved is not a defect.
The move directly addresses explanatory standards and rejects the inference from an unanswered cosmic origin to the need for a theistic worldview.
The audience question challenges how Matt can hold a worldview that lacks an explanation for the origin of the universe.
Matt offers several open possibilities for why anything exists and argues that claiming a total explanation from discomfort with uncertainty is epistemically irresponsible.
Continuing disagreement does not disprove God, but an unfalsifiable god claim can persist indefinitely because believers need not provide supporting evidence.
The move clarifies Matt's objection to the god proposition as unfalsifiable while avoiding the invalid claim that persistent debate itself proves nonexistence.
The audience asks whether an ongoing debate about God should imply that God does not exist.
Matt charitably reconstructs the audience question, distinguishes proof from non-disproof, and explains why unsupported unfalsifiable claims can remain believed without resolution.
Ray's demand for a humble heart amounts to asking for an unskeptical mind, whereas reasonable belief requires demonstrable evidence rather than submission.
The move exposes a core conflict between spiritual receptivity and evidential scrutiny, challenging Ray's explanation for why nonbelievers reject the gospel.
Ray describes people who listen with a humble and open heart as appropriately receptive to the gospel.
Matt denies that his skepticism is prideful, reframes the issue as epistemology, and maintains that unsupported claims cannot reasonably command belief.
God's existence is self-evident, salvation is promised to genuine seekers, and trusting God is more secure than the ordinary forms of faith used throughout life.
The move combines Ray's claims about universal awareness of God, the conditions of salvation, and faith as the appropriate response to the gospel promise.
The audience question asks whether God's failure to appear clearly to someone should suggest that God does not care.
Ray says creation gives everyone knowledge of God, attributes unsuccessful appeals to inadequate trust, and contrasts fallible everyday objects of trust with God's unfailing promise.
Trust in trained professionals is proportioned to demonstrated competence, institutional safeguards, and available evidence, unlike trust in God.
The move disputes a principal defense of religious trust by distinguishing evidence-supported practical reliance from confidence in an unverified deity.
Ray Comfort's comparison of faith in God with ordinary reliance on pilots, doctors, medicines, traffic controls, and brakes.
After Comfort argues that everyday life routinely requires faith, Dillahunty distinguishes regulated and evidence-calibrated trust from the religious confidence Comfort advocates.
Claims that God saves those who call on him are insulated from disconfirmation by treating every apparent failure as defective belief or false conversion.
The move alleges that the salvation promise lacks falsifiable consequences because unfavorable outcomes can always be reassigned to the petitioner's sincerity.
Ray Comfort's claim that God reliably saves sincere seekers and that an apparent failure usually shows that the person did not truly trust.
Dillahunty develops his evidential objection by arguing that Comfort adds qualifications after the fact, preventing failed salvation experiences from counting against the promise.
The skeptical position is supported by argument and evidence, whereas Comfort's position relies on assertions and labels contrary conclusions as mere belief.
This move crystallizes the debate's epistemic dispute by alleging an asymmetry between evidence-based criticism and unsupported theological assertion.
Ray Comfort's dismissal of Dillahunty's preceding evidential criticism as simply Dillahunty's own belief.
Following Comfort's brief dismissal, Dillahunty defends his conclusion as argued and evidenced, accuses Comfort of unsupported assertion, and demands a counter-demonstration.
People need not independently judge God's goodness because God's sinlessness, the truth of scripture, and humanity's evident moral danger warrant complete trust in him.
The move directly defends the moral authority and trustworthiness of God, which bears on whether the gospel's account of judgment and salvation makes moral sense.
Answering whether humans can judge God's justice and goodness, Comfort grounds trust in divine sinlessness, scriptural teaching about human evil, and widespread religious experience.
